title: When two words sound the same
goal: How one global solve decides who keeps a stroke: spelling, the star ladder, the marker stroke and names.

blocks.x: One primary stroke per word

A word gets exactly one primary single-stroke outline: never a choice between several to learn. This page covers only *which* word keeps a stroke when two or more want it. The extra one-stroke forms a word gets afterwards only take strokes this settling left free. Multi-stroke backups are separate and unlimited: see [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).
Everything is settled together

Briefs, spelling and the star ladder are not three passes. Every word's full set of legal candidates goes into one shared pool, and a single solve picks the assignment that minimizes the whole dictionary's total cost at once, weighted by how often each word is said. The candidates of a word are:

items: a gold brief of its own (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs)), if it keys the first onset or pays for itself (see [faithful outlines](#/ref/collisions));
lyk's plain rules reading;
the spelling-told-apart variant for its sound-alike group (see [spelling](#/ref/spelling));
every brevity-shortened form (see [how short](#/ref/brevity));
the full star ladder, below;
for a word spelled with a literal trailing `s`, the same candidate again with a voiced `-Z` coda respelled `-S`.

blocks.x: The letter is decided by cost per word, not by a blanket rule: *girls* is [[girls|TKPWEURLS]] with its [[-Z]] reading [[girls|TKPWEURLZ]] kept as an extra, and *abhors* is [[abhors|PWHORS]].
A common word can lose an outline to another word if that makes the whole dictionary cheaper, and a rare word's situation can move a common word to its next-cheapest candidate.
Faithful outlines: a dropped sound must pay

Plover's and Lapwing's briefs often leave out a sound at the start of the word: *grab* as `RAB`, *graph* as `TPWRAF` (a `G` with no `K`), *got* as `TKPOT` (a `G` as `TKP`). An outline is **faithful** when it writes every sound of the word's first onset with that sound's own keys, as the tables write them: `G` is all of `TKPW`, `J` is all of `SKWR`, `gr` is `TKPWR`, `bl` is `PWHR`. Vowels, the star, extra keys and the whole right hand are not part of the check. A sound at the end of the word may still be dropped: [[find|TPAOEUD]] keys the F, the vowel and the D, and not the N.
A gold outline that is unfaithful (as listed, or with its fragments dropped) is a candidate only if it **pays for itself**, in one of three ways:

items: **It saves a whole stroke.** It takes fewer strokes than every other candidate the word has. The cost ranks strokes first, then keys, so a drop that saves only keys within one stroke is never worth it: `TPWRAF` and the faithful `TKPWRAF` are both one stroke, so the faithful one wins. A long word whose faithful reading takes two or more strokes may still drop a sound for one: [[request|KW]], [[describe|SKREU]].

**The word is among the commonest.** Its rank is below `faithful_exempt_rank` in `rules/plover.toml` (550). The commonest words keep their short briefs (*the*, *of*, *you*, and also *make* `AEUBG`, *day* `AEU`, *give* `EUF`). A family member past that rank follows its root only if the root's shape keys the onset too. Several common words that drop a whole onset therefore stay as they were: *great* `RAET`, *guy* `TKPAOEU`, *gone* `OPB`, *give* `EUF`, *gave* `AEUF`. Pinning *great* to `TKPWRAET` was measured and fails the Gutenberg guard (7.3% of words cost more than Plover) at ranks 550 and 650.
**A human pinned it.** A literal `[word]` outline in `rules/briefs.toml` (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs)), or a source named there, is always allowed. [[got|TKPWOT]] and [[find|TPAOEUD]] are pinned.

blocks.x: The rules' own reading is faithful by definition. The brevity ladder's one-stroke short forms (`shell`, `ends`, vowel-less skeleton, see [how short](#/ref/brevity)) are not held to it: they save a stroke, as they always did. A faithful outline can lose its stroke to a word that sounds the same, as any outline can: *graph* is [[graph|TKPWRAFR]] because the name *graff* holds `TKPWRAF`.
The exemption rank, measured

These rows were measured with Plover and Lapwing as the only sources, before [other theories' briefs](#/ref/collisions) joined the pool. The ordering and the guard's cut-off at 550 are the same with them, but the absolute numbers below are those of the earlier pool.

The stroke count never moves, and the taught set stays at 98.5%. Keys per word are what faithful onsets cost: 550 adds 0.02 keys a word (0.6%) and 1.2% comfort. What stops the exemption going lower is the Gutenberg-prose guard in the test suite (at most 7.2% of words may cost more keys than Plover): at rank 500 it reads 7.2% rounded, just over, at 550 it passes. The keys-per-word guard (3.272 with 2% slack) holds at every rank in the table.
Other theories' briefs

Besides Plover and Lapwing, the generator reads fifteen more dictionaries as a pool of briefs: Stan's (a derivative of Magnum, the theory of Mark Kislingbury), Josiah theory (a write-short theory with a dictionary of about 30,000 plain words; the outlines on its own extra `^` key do not exist on this layout and are skipped) and thirteen court-reporting theories published by Stenovations: Bryan, StarTran, Steno Foundation, The Steno Way, Tri-C, Pennsylvania Clinic, RealWrite, Robert Walsh Gonzales, San Antonio, South Coast College, StenEd, Stenograph and Thyra Ellis. Each is `data/dictionaries/theory-NAME.json`, downloaded by `fetch`; every `theory-*.json` file found is merged into one list of outlines per word (`Gold::extra`). Magnum's own dictionary is sold with its book, Platinum's is a members' download, and Palantype is another layout, so they are not in the pool.

**Their outlines are held to one rule: they must save a stroke.** An outline from these theories is a candidate only if it takes fewer strokes than every other candidate the word has (under any of its pronunciations), the rules' own reading included. They never replace a one-stroke outline the word already has. Neither the commonest-words exemption nor a faithful onset gets one in: a word that already fits one stroke keeps what Plover, Lapwing or the rules gave it. Without the rule a dozen theories handed *job* `KWROB`, *liquid* `KHREUD` and *dock* `TKAUBG`, each a key shorter and none predictable. What the rule buys is one-stroke words: *accuracy* (`ABG/+SEU` before) is now [[accuracy|KRAES]], *added* (`AD/+-D`) is [[added|ATD]].

The cost is on the reading side. More words sit on irregular one-stroke briefs (*penguin* `PEPBG`, *incomplete* `*EUBG`), so the solver's weighted top-1 on backups falls a point (92.7% to 91.7%) and each stroke carries more keys; the comfort per word is 0.4 worse. The taught outlines do not move. Plover's `PWHR-G` and similar family shapes can also change hands: [[assembling|PWHR-G]] is one stroke now, so *building* is [[building|PW-LG]]. The Gutenberg-prose and keys-per-word guards hold unchanged.

**What does not save a stroke is still used, as an alternate.** The extras pass (the last one, which only fills strokes nobody holds) also reads the other theories' one-stroke outlines for a word: the first onset must be keyed, no half of a multi-key sound may be in it, and it must be typable on lyk's layout (some theories use chords this layout cannot press). It adds them within three keys of the word's own outline, at most three extras per word with the word's own. They never become a primary, never take a stroke, and never change a word's cheapest outline. About 1,000 alternates were added this way (24,652 to 25,672 extras); the other theories hold about 22,000 more unused one-stroke outlines, almost all for words that already have a one-stroke lyk outline, and the filters, the three-extras cap and the key margin leave them out. Their multi-stroke outlines (about 219,000 unused) are not read at all; they were not sampled for quality.
What spelling decides

Spelling answers "who may even propose this word's plain, unstressed-vowel reading", not "who should win it". *sail* (`!ai`) and *sale* (silent e) sound identical but spell the stressed vowel differently, so the rules write two outlines: [[sail|SAEUL]] for the `!ai` spelling and the shorter [[sale|SAEL]] for the silent e. Both are candidates for their words. Which gets the longer or the shorter form is decided by the same cost-and-frequency solve, which usually gives the commoner member of a pair the cheaper pick. See [spelling](#/ref/spelling) for how a sound becomes a spelling-told-apart variant.
The star ladder

When two words with the same spelling pattern want one stroke, the commoner one keeps the plain stroke and the other falls down a ladder of its own. Every word always carries these four steps in its candidate pool alongside everything else, so a word that loses an outline falls to its next-cheapest option inside the same solve:

items: a star on the first stroke;
a star on the last stroke;
one extra star-marker stroke, [[+*]] after the outline;
two extra star-marker strokes.

blocks.x: Examples: [[night|TPHAOEUT]] and [[knight|TPHAO*EUT]]; [[flower|TPHROUR]] and [[flour|TPHRO*UR]]; [[pearl|PERL]] and [[peril|P*ERL]]; [[sweet|SWAOET]] and [[sweetie|SWAO*ET]].
A short form never takes an outline that any word's own rules produce. The forms a learner can work out stay theirs.
A star on a one-syllable stroke means the sound-alike

*doc* is [[doc|TKOBG]], so *dock* is [[dock|TKO*BG]]. *sock* is [[sock|SO*BG]] (and [[sobbing|SOBG]] is *sob* plus `-G`). A longer word's short form pays half a stroke on top of its cost to take a one-syllable stroke's star. A short form with another one-stroke form a key or two dearer leaves the star to the sound-alike. One that would otherwise be two strokes and is said far more often keeps it: *attack* is [[attack|TA*BG]], so *tack* is [[tack|TABG/+*]].
What a word falls to, in order
Cost decides, so the order is strokes first, then keys:

items: its own one-stroke reading;
a star on it;
a gold brief of its own that is still one stroke;

among two-stroke forms, the cheapest of: its stem-plus-suffix reading (*pearly* [[pearly|PERL/+EU]], once [[PERL]] is *pearl* and [[P*ERL]] is *peril*), a two-stroke gold brief, and its reading with one bare [[+*]] marker stroke.

blocks.x: The marker stroke is the last resort of a one-syllable word. It is a rule, not a memorised fact: a stroke that is taken, starred and still taken, is written again with [[+*]] after it. *suite* is [[suite|SWAOET/+*]] because [[SWAOET]] is *sweet* and [[SWAO*ET]] is *sweetie*. About 1,200 words end that way, almost all names and interjections (*uhh* [[uhh|U/+*]], *hah* [[hah|HA/+*]]).
Names

A name never outranks the word it sounds like. lyk writes a name as the ordinary outline of how it sounds, after the capitalize stroke [[KPA]]: *Matt* is [[KPA]] then *mat*'s stroke. A name and its sound-alike word compete for one stroke, and the word should have it, since the name gets its capital from [[KPA]] either way.

items: Each name's count is cut to a tenth before anything is ranked. A common name still outranks a rare word.
A name here is a word Plover and Lapwing only ever write capitalized (*Matt*, *Mike*, *Mary*, *America*, *Sunday*), never lowercase.
*mat* is [[mat|PHAT]] and *matt* is [[matt|PHAT/+*]].

Some names lose their one-stroke outline this way and are typed by their syllables like any two-syllable word: *mary* is [[mary|PHAER/+EU]], since *marry* has [[marry|PHAER]] and *merry* has [[merry|PH*ER]].
